speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-53, an Act to amend the Supreme Court Act and to amend various other Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
There are five motions at the report stage of Bill C-53, an Act to amend the Supreme Court Act and to amend various other Acts in consequence thereof, standing in the name of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn).
All of these motions deal with the elimination of gender references and all were asked for my members of the legislative committee which considered this Bill.

I am given to understand that these amendments have been proposed at the committee stage. However the drafters of the Bill were not prepared to proceed at that time.

All of the motions are in order and will be debated together. If a division is required, a division on Motion No. 1 will be applied to Motion Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 5. The House will now proceed to debate Motion Nos. 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.

Madam Speaker, I would like to indicate that we support these amendments, but in

October 23, 1987
Supreme Court Act
offering our support and our part of the unanimous consent required I would like the Minister to notice how easy these amendments were to achieve, and to remind him of the commitment which was made in connection with the statute consolidations that gender neutrality would be sought.
On behalf of the Liberal Party, I indicated that we recognize that there were cases where gender neutrality, because of the limitations of the English language and the rules of grammar, sometimes has too high a price and that in the revising of a statute, particularly a criminal statute, to remove the gender orientation of a pronoun sometimes makes the language so complicated that it is hard for a citizen to understand. 1 indicated for our part that we were sympathetic to that kind of problem and that we were not insisting that every "his" and "him" be removed.
The ease with which these changes were achieved in these five cases shows that there has been a half-hearted effort to apply the general policy of avoiding "his" and "him" in the language of legislation. It does not sound like a very big issue, whether "him" or "his" appear in a statute or whether that can be avoided in the English language.

And for francophones who may be interested, the problem does not arise because the grammar is different and the gender of the pronoun depends on the following noun rather than the subject.

For Anglophones, it is important. The Minister and some of his colleagues are supporting a conference that 1 attended last night, to which I was very glad to be invited, of the National Association for Women and the Law. The indignation which one feels over the situation of women under the criminal law in general is so immense, and there is so much substance to their grievance that this type of change we are considering today is hardly responsive. It is very small, yet it is important symbolically.
In agreeing with these changes, 1 want to criticize the fact that it was even necessary to mention them and that the Government was not following its policy of doing everything that could reasonably be done with the English language to avoid getting into this situation in the first place. These amendments have our support and we concur in the unanimous consent required to receive them at this time.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I am pleased today to speak on behalf of the New Democratic Party, being a critic of everything these days, expert on nothing. However, I am pleased to see that the Minister has cleaned up his sexist language. He called it "gender neutral", which I think is the proper term.
I note that the Minister had a little assistance, as usual, from the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) who when speaking in this House on September 14, 1987 said, as reported in Hansard, at page 8920:
I was pleased to hear the undertaking of the Minister that he intends to support an amendment to delete those odious provisions. I made strong representations to the Minister on this point. I indicated that I intend to propose an amendment to delete this provision and I welcome his agreement to support my amendment and agree to the deletion of this very backward and regressive provision of the legislation.
1 am pleased to see that the Minister, although he did not say so in his introductory remarks, is bringing forward our amendments. 1 would hope the Justice Department would not require, under its very able Deputy Minister, that the Minister be forced to rise to bring these amendments to this kind of legislation. As the Liberal critic said, they should know enough by now to bring that in in the first place, but we thank them for the fact that they did and 1 am pleased on behalf of our party to support these amendments.

He said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to address the House today on third reading of Bill C-53. At the outset, 1 want to acknowledge the assistance of Hon. Members who have taken an interest in these amendments and in particular to express my appreciation to the members of the legislative committee who considered the Bill in a thoughtful and timely manner.
When I rose to speak on Bill C-53 at second reading, 1 indicated that I would be bringing forward amendments to the Bill to preserve the present practice regarding appeals as of right. That commitment was fulfilled at the legislative
October 23, 1987

committee and was supported by all members of the committee. I also brought to the attention of the committee certain statistics dealing with the current workload of the court in order to demonstrate the need for the provision in Bill C-53 regarding applications for leave to appeal.
Bill C-53 is a step forward in many respects. It will benefit counsel, litigants and the court itself through the changes to the Supreme Court Act dealing with the delivery of judgments and the time periods for bringing appeals and applications for leave to appeal. As well, the amendments which deal with fairness and security are positive changes. The legislation will now provide the Supreme Court of Canada with the authority to assign counsel to an unrepresented accused.
We must give our highest court the tools it needs to carry out its responsibility. We are, as 1 have stated before on several occasions, well served by the men and women who sit on the Supreme Court of Canada. Their ability and integrity is well known to all of us. They are faced, on a daily basis, with the challenge of interpreting our Constitution and with fundamental legal issues of national importance that affect all Canadians.
This Bill will be a help to the court in discharging its role and in marshalling its time effectively to address these matters of such great importance.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 also am very pleased to be able to support this Bill and to have it pass through the process of the House of Commons expeditiously and in a great spirit of co-operation. That co-operation included acceptance by the Minister not only of amendments this morning but important amendments in committee. It is certain that Canadians are very proud of the highest court in this land and that is a tribute to the calibre of people that sit on it, the way in which they work, and the support they have had from Governments of Canada, present and past.
When the amendment package was proposed it was important for us to be satisfied that it would improve the court. We were concerned, as I indicated, about some constrictions on access by Canadians to the highest court. We wanted to be certain that they were justified and necessary. It is true that this country's lawyers, through their organizations, indicated they were happy with the Bill the way it was.
The Minister told us as well that there had been consultations in the proper manner with members of the Supreme Court of Canada. He indicated in committee that they were content with the proposed changes. Of course, there is more to it than that. There is the point of view of the citizens of Canada and that is the job of this House. We accepted that the Bar was happy, the Bench was happy, but were the changes satisfactory from the point of view of the citizens of Canada?
We have dealt with the amendments on gender neutrality and I have spoken about those already. I am glad to see them
Supreme Court Act
included in the law. I would also point out that we were not happy with the restriction of the appeal by right which existed under the old law and which would have been taken away under the Bill proposed by the Government. Therefore we are glad that the Government agreed that this right would continue as before in at least a couple of respects. It means that someone who has had an adverse judgment and over which there was some disagreement among judges on the way up will have an appeal of right. This right was restored at our urging as well as the urging of a number of the media and public interest groups across the country, as I think the Minister would acknowledge.
We have before us a Bill which changes the rules somewhat. For example, it reduces to a certain degree the visibility of the Supreme Court of Canada because it will now be handing down written judgments rather than giving them orally in open court. Certain arguments for leave to appeal which were formally argued in open court and in front of the public and the media may now take place on paper without the necessity of an oral hearing. This will save money, yes; it will save time, it is true. However, it takes something away from the visibility of the court. On the other hand, the reason we supported these amendments was because we felt and continue to feel that the time of the court is a precious asset of the Canadian people and we have to be certain that it is used wisely and well.

So we were and we are still prepared to support the Bill as amended, and hopefully Canadians will accept the few restrictions imposed through this measure. But at the same time as we have so spared the precious time of the court-the most important in Canada-to safeguard our rights and freedoms, we readily admit that the Supreme Court of Canada has such a heavy workload and is under so much pressure that indeed an attempt must be made to save time and make better use of it. In conclusion I would say that we are quite pleased to support the Government by way of the amendments we have proposed. We hope the Bill will be sent to the Senate and that we will soon have the kind of legislation as envisaged in these amendments.

Mir. Ian Waddell (Vancouver-Kingsway):	Madam
Speaker, I would like to speak to this matter on third reading. I did not have the advantage of attending meetings of the committee but I understand the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) is quite correct when he paid tribute to members of that committee. Indeed, this seems to be a good example of Parliament at work in the sense that some amendments have been accepted and some rejected. That is the way it should work.
1 believe this is the first Bill to come before this House in a long time which deals in a substantive way with the Supreme Court of Canada. The court is very important, and right now very busy. I can see the court's problem and that of the

October 23, 1987
Supreme Court Act
Minister of Justice because he is responsible for the administration of justice in that court. His problem lies in trying to bring in reform of an extremely busy court, reform which will not restrict too much the people's right of appeal.
All the cases that appear before this court are important. They are also very visible. The Thatcher case and the Morgen-taler case are two examples. The Charter of Rights has made things even more difficult for the court. Of course, when the Meech Lake Accord goes through the court will have an even larger workload with which to deal. However, I will not get into that today.
To get back to the Bill, the amendments that the Liberal critic and the Minister spoke about, concerning not restricting the right of appeal if in fact a judge on the way up, as it was put, registered a dissent, restore that right of appeal to the highest court of the country. I think it was wise to allow that procedure to continue.
If the Minister will forgive me for a moment, 1 would just tell him that when I started in law 1 was a community lawyer in Vancouver. A woman came through my door one day. She was on bail, having been charged with the murder of her husband in Burns Lake, British Columbia. It was a very tragic case. She did not have a lawyer and asked me if 1 would take the case. I took the case. It was my first murder case. I went to Burns Lake for the preliminary hearing and to Prince Rupert for the trial where she was acquitted. The Crown appealed. I will never forget getting the notice on the twenty-eighth day. The case went to the Supreme Court of British Columbia where we lost, two to one. Former Chief Justice Ferris dissented. The great happiness of the acquittal in Prince Rupert turned into great sadness at the loss in the Court of Appeal in Vancouver. However, because there was a dissenter, we were entitled as of right to go to the Supreme Court of Canada. I am happy to tell the Minister of Justice that we won in the Supreme Court of Canada.
That is a concrete example of what 1 am talking about. Had this woman not had the right to appeal she could stand convicted of murder today or, at the very minimum, have gone through another long trial. I believe that justice was done in that case.
I acknowledge that there is a problem. The Supreme Court of Canada judges are extremely overworked. I want to pay tribute to them. We have an excellent Bench in the Supreme Court. They are very hard-working Canadians.
However, all is not sweetness and light. The Government retained the provision that you do not have the right to an oral hearing on the appeal. That may have been a bit of a compromise. The Government may have thought that since the court is so busy it had to cut back somehow. However, as 1 understand it, if you file for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court you do not necessarily get an oral hearing. You can do it by written submissions.
I want to quote the words of Thomas Berger, a distinguished lawyer in British Columbia who was a member of the Supreme Court of British Columbia for 11 years. These words were quoted by my colleague, the Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), on September 14, 1987, in this House as reported on page 8917 of Hansard. Mr. Berger said:
To reduce the whole matter to paper seems to me to downgrade the role of advocacy; this is not in keeping with the traditions of our bar.
It is not simply that this contributes to the openness of the justice system at the very highest level; my argument is that it enables the court better to understand the exact question that is before it. This contributes to better decision making.
I believe that in spite of the understandable difficulties of a very busy court, it would be better to provide in law that those seeking leave to appeal to the highest court of the land have the opportunity to present their application orally, in person or through counsel, for the reasons set out by former Judge Berger, that it does keep the openness in our justice system at a very high level. It also enables the court to understand the case better. Sometimes you have to hear counsel, to get the words up from the paper in order to appreciate that there is a question of justice.
That is what the courts are about when all is said and done, when all the law is applied, all the paperwork is put through, and all the cases are cited, read, and reread. That is what courts are about in a free society. When a good judge and a good court see a situation which is not just, they will find a way of making it just. That is the best part of our legal system. There are bad parts of our legal system as well, but that is the best part. That is why we should agree only reluctantly to a cut-back in oral presentations to the Supreme Court on applications for leave.
There are other provisions in this Bill to which 1 have no objection, such as depositing copies of judgments with the registrar so that the full court does not have to appear to give judgment, reference to time limits, and so on.
I think we should consider the views of the Supreme Court judges with regard to appeal, their workload, and what the court is doing. I think it is appropriate in the constitutional system to have more contact with the Supreme Court judges, the court, and the Justice Committee, perhaps on an informal basis, so that parliamentarians get an understanding of what the Supreme Court is doing. In the last five years we have consistently, through the Charter of Rights and other laws, given more and more work to the Supreme Court of Canada.
In conclusion, I do disapprove of that part of the Bill. 1 suggest that Members may want to read the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Burnaby, our justice critic, on September 14, 1987 in this House, as well as the remarks of the Member for St. John's East (Mr. Harris) who is also a lawyer and spoke in this debate as well. He shared some of his experience in the courts.

Madam Speaker, I would like to respond to the question put to me yesterday by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) as reported at page 10300 of Hansard. The Member seemed upset that I had not mentioned in my speech the Canada-U.S. agreement with regard to the chemical dump along the American side of the Niagara River. It is indeed a very important environmental concern.
However, it is also important to draw to the attention of the House that it was a former Liberal Government that started negotiations with the American Government to try to find a solution to this environmental concern. In October, 1984, after many months of negotiations, the Canada-U.S. Niagara River Toxic Committee published its report. Three years have passed since then. This is a plan on paper only with no funding from either side. There has been very little pressure on the part of Canada to have the Americans clean up the pollution on their side of the Niagara River. I am still concerned that there have not been any real, concrete measures taken at this time. That is what 1 was trying to explain in my speech yesterday.
We also know that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has had some difficulties either with Treasury Board or the estimates of his own department. Over the years
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
his department has been subject to cuts. There has been a cutback of 106 person-years and in three years the Tory Government has removed $64 million in spending power, so his departmental estimates have not kept up with inflation.
We know that the cut-back in person-years has had an effect on pollution studies and control of toxic substances which may find their way into the food chain. For example, one scientist has been assigned to the Niagara study. I do not believe that is sufficient for a very urgent and important problem that must be resolved.
Yesterday, my hon. friend expressed surprise at my not giving him and his Government all the kudos he would like. I had to be somewhat apprehensive about-

-the political will and indeed the decision-making power of this Government to take action so that the Niagara River, like the St. Clair River and all others which flow in this country- yesterday 1 mentioned the Ottawa River-and which are under stress, if I may put it that way, toxic stress ... As far as I am concerned, Madam Speaker, we must take action immediately, make the necessary appropriations, hire the required staff and scientists and provide them with whatever tools they need to clean up our rivers and settle the problem.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to Bill C-74 today. I believe this Bill is the most important piece of federal environmental protection legislation to come before the House in the last 10 years.
Today, as we wind down second reading, I propose that we get back to what really matters in this debate, the purpose of Bill C-74 and what it will do for Canada and Canadians.
During this debate the House has heard a number of unfounded observations on the part of the Opposition. Before proceeding to rebut some of those criticisms I want to set the record straight as to the objectives and purposes of this Bill. Canadians are anxiously waiting for the passage of this legislation in order that we may get on with the job of better protecting our environment. As far as protection of our environment is concerned, this Government subscribes to the concept of "anticipate and prevent". As a result of Canada's failure in the past to enhance the principle of prevention, we all know too well that problems have come back to haunt us.
One such threat has become a component of our daily life, toxic chemicals. We live in a global chemical society. We plow chemicals into our fields, release them into the air, treat our food with them, wear them, and use them in thousands of products. Each day Canadians enjoy a quality of life enhanced by but dependent on the use of chemicals. Life without chemicals has become virtually impossible, perhaps unthinkable. The benefits to Canadians from chemicals are significant. They are also immediate. However, our short term benefits are creating a long term legacy of continuing problems. We must

October 23, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
be sure that we do not make decisions today that cause problems for tomorrow's generations.
Bill C-74 also concerns protecting the Canadian environment from damage before the fact. The Canadian environmental protection legislation provides for an investigation to determine the potential impact of a new substance before it enters the Canadian commerce. Without the new Act, Canadians would continue to be at risk from toxic chemicals. Biologically engineered substances would still pose a threat until an indisputable case of environmental or human damage could be demonstrated. This could be years after the release of the substance into our environment. The Canadian Environmental Protection Act is designed to prevent another PCB or chlorofluorocarbon problem in this country.
Bill C-74 provides greater information gathering powers for the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan). It will be possible for the Minister to obtain data on other uses of a substance, precautions for safe handling, recommended methods of disposal, and safety measures to be taken in case of an accident. He will be able to assess whether a substance new to Canada or one already existing in Canadian commerce is toxic or may become toxic. The Minister may collect data and conduct investigations on the nature of that substance as well. He may seek out the effect of its presence on the environment, on human life and health, as well as the extent to which the substance can become dispersed and will persist in the environment.
In addition, the Minister may collect data on the ability of the substance to become incorporated into biological tissue and cause biological change, important for both environmental and health reasons. He may additionally investigate methods of controlling the presence of the substance in the environment and methods for testing the effects of its presence.
These powers to gather information feed into all important aspects of Bill C-74 that allow control of all aspects of the life cycle of toxic substances, from development through manufacture or importation, transport, distribution, storage and use, their release to the environment as emissions at various stages of the life cycle, and their ultimate disposal as waste.
Bill C-74 goes even further in its provision for environmental controls. The responsibilities of the various federal bodies are also underscored in this piece of legislation. It allows for adoption of regulations governing federal works and to protect federal lands and water where not currently provided for. In keeping with the federal team approach to protection of our environment, federal departments and agencies are looking at environmental considerations in their program development. They are scanning legislation to see where there are gaps that the Canadian environmental protection Bill can plug successfully.
The Government of Canada intends to set the example for other Canadian jurisdictions. In keeping with the concept of "anticipate and prevent", the new Act will require the Minister of the Environment to create environmental quality
objectives and guidelines as well as guidelines for the release of substances and codes of practice. The objectives, guidelines and codes will relate to recycling, reusing, treating, storing, disposing of and reducing the release of substances. It is in this area that the Government of Canada is counting on extensive co-operation with provincial and territorial governments and with industry. This is in keeping with the traditional partnership and consultative approach that Environment Canada has used almost since its creation as a department about 15 years ago.
In the area of Canada's international commitment, Bill C-74 contains provisions to control sources of air pollution in Canada where a violation of an international agreement would result. This would also be applicable where air pollution affects another country and reciprocal legislation exists to control the sources of that pollution.
Provisions under the current Ocean Dumping Control Act will be incorporated into the Bill. These provisions will allow issuance of permits to control dumping at sea from ships, barges, aircraft and man-made structures, excluding normal discharges from offshore energy facilities. This will maintain Canada's federal domestic legislation that fulfills our international commitments under the London Dumping Convention. There are also provisions incorporated from the Canada Water Act for the control of nutrients such as phosphates water conditioners or cleaning products. Natural amounts of nutrients such as phosphates that enter the environment are not toxic. However, excessive amounts of nutrients can interfere with the use of fresh water by humans, animals, fish and plants.
One very important component of Bill C-74 is the provision allowing for agreements to be signed with the provincial and territorial governments for administration of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. There has already been preliminary discussions with provinces and territories, individually and among federal and provincial environment Ministers, at meetings of the Canadian Council for Resource and Environment Ministers.
There have been suggestions in the House that the federal Government is going to use these agreements to abandon the field, so to speak, as far as enforcement of the Environmental Protection Act is concerned. An essential feature of any agreement signed with the province or territory will be the enforcement and compliance policy for the Act. Such a document was released in draft form for public consultation on June 26 of this year. Provinces and territories that sign agreements for administration of the new legislation will be required to adhere to that policy. These agreements, in order to ensure nationally consistent enforcement, will also spell out procedures for audit and evaluation of enforcement and compliance activities under the Act.
October 23, 1987

During the debate, it has also been stated that each province has been given a veto over the application of the Act in its jurisdiction if the province feels it has comparable legislation. This is simply not the case. No provision of Bill C-74 gives any veto to provinces or territories. Under Canada's Constitution, the provinces, of course, do have responsibilities to protect the environment. In that regard, the Minister must offer to consult with them on proposed regulations that would govern releases of toxic substances to the environment.
We must also offer to consult with provinces on regulation development in such areas as manufacturing, commercial and processing activities giving rise to these releases, and storage, display, handling, transport and disposal of toxic substances. But 1 think this is simply a confirmation in legislation of the manner in which this Government conducts its business, that is, with extensive consultation. However, a requirement to consult does not imply a provincial veto. The Government of Canada still retains the right to act to protect the environment.
We have heard some disappointment expressed that pesticides and chemicals used in foods are not included in the proposed Bill. There is currently in place both federal legislation and a regulatory system for pesticides under the Pest Control Products Act administered by Agriculture Canada. That Act provides for control over the manufacture, storage, display, labelling, distribution and use of pesticides in this country. The Environmental Protection Act is designed to complement the Pest Control Products Act and not to make it redundant. Therefore, in areas where the substance is not regulated under other Acts, the Canadian Environmental Protection Act will apply. For example, if the pesticide was being manufactured or imported for use as a flame retardant, Bill C-74 would apply.
The same would be true if the pesticide appeared on the list of substances requiring pre-export notification to a receiving country. Where this is a matter of toxic affluence from pesticides, a leak or spill, or toxic pesticide wastes which are not dealt with specifically in the Pest Control Products Act, a regulation could be made under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. As well, of course, appropriate provincial legislation may come into play.
While pesticides remain under the Pest Control Products Act, this does not mean that Environment Canada has no role to play in this field. In addition, Environment Canada, like the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, acts as a technical adviser to Agriculture Canada in the registration process. Environment is also involved in monitoring the fate of pesticides in the environment, of course.
The Minister of the Environment considers his Department's role in the pesticides area so important that he has secured and allocated seven additional person-years and yearly funds of $3.2 million to ensure complete and comprehensive environmental evaluations of pesticide products. His Department's
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
research and monitoring program, which will provide necessary environmental data to undertake regulatory evaluation of pesticides, began in 1986 and is making, I understand, all hope for progress.
Another criticism of the Bill is the omission of a statement which would prohibit the export of substances banned in Canada. This Bill calls for compulsory notification for export of regulated substances. This is consistent with requirements of the United Nations Environment Program and with criteria laid down by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, both endorsed by this country.
We will, of course, require that export of banned or regulated substances be preceded by compulsory notification of the receiving country on the occasion of the first export shipment. It will then be up to the receiving country to determine compliance with its laws.
While the export of these substances will not currently be prohibited under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, Canada could take that step because the proposed Act does allow the making of regulations for the total, partial or conditional export of a substance or product containing that substance. But we should not forget that the banning or restriction of a substance in Canada would have to be done under the Act after taking into account affects on our environment or the health of our residents.
The same environmental conditions and health factors might not come into play in countries with completely different climates, vegetation, pest and parasitic problems, and the like. Those countries may have a use, even a need, for the very substance which Canada has chosen to restrict or ban in this country under our Environmental Protection Act. It is for this reason that an outright prohibition of the exported substances banned or restricted in Canada does not appear in Bill C-74.
Several speakers have decried the absence of an Environmental bill of rights for all Canadians. The rights of individuals have been addressed in this Bill. There is extensive opportunity for public participation and enforcement of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. For instance, a person subject to loss or damage as a result of an action prohibited by the statute has the right to seek an injunction in the courts to stop or prevent the action. Any 12 persons can petition the Minister to investigate an alleged offence. The Minister has an obligation to report his findings.
When reporting to an inspector or other official the alleged release, leaked, spilled, dumping, and so on, of a substance to the environment, a person has the right to have his or her identity kept confidential. Individuals may petition the Minister to have a substance included on the list of priority substances to be studied and the Minister must respond with his decision.
A person may appeal a decision not to regulate a substance as toxic and that appeal will be considered by a board of review. Individuals will have the opportunity to appear before

October 23, 1987
boards of review established under the Act and a board of review will be empowered to award costs to those appearing before it.
One element requested for inclusion in an environmental bill of rights, namely, standing and access to the courts, is a right already enjoyed by Canadians. Private individuals have the right to prosecute federal summary conviction offences.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION OF INDIGENOUS PEOPLES-REVISION OF CONVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the 152 member states of the International Labour Organization, the ILO, are in the process of revising a Convention which was approved 30 years ago concerning the protection of indigenous peoples in independent countries. The Government of Canada must send to the ILO by October 31 its response to the proposed revisions. Although the deadline is just a week away, and although the ILO directed its member states to ensure the participation of their indigenous peoples in the revision process, so far Canada has refused to share its draft response with indigenous peoples here.
In view of the importance of this Convention to the indigenous peoples of Canada-it is the only existing international Convention providing for their protection in the area of labour relations, land use and ownership, and social and cultural rights-and the opportunity this process of revision offers Canada to play a leading role internationally, I request the Government to provide a text to the indigenous peoples immediately so that their views can be incorporated into Canada's response.

subtopic: PORT WELLER DRY DOCKS-AWARDING OF REFIT CONTRACT URGED
PORT WELLER DRY DOCKS-AWARDING OF REFIT CONTRACT URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for years the shipbuilders of Canada have been crying out for a national shipbuilding strategy. They desperately need policies to encourage a sourcing of vessels at home.
There is high demand for Atlantic fishing trawlers, and there are military requirements of a big and small nature. There is the ongoing replacement and the expansion of the Canadian Coast Guard.
Yards have been restructured, improved to meet that demand, some with federal government assistance and some without. Such rationalization or restructuring does not in itself bring in new business. Much of it is by way of allocation. The Government must recognize the Canada-wide employment needs and technical development opportunities that shipbuilding and its allied industries bring.
Port Weller Dry Docks in St. Catharines, the last Canadian shipbuilding yard on the Great Lakes, is reduced to a skeleton staff. Hundreds of dry dock workers are on layoff. This is at a time when a press report indicates that an Atlantic seaboard yard speaks of full employment and orders not yet begun.
It is a timely opportunity for the Government to demonstrate sensitivity to the region of Niagara and award the midlife refit of the Ontario-based Coast Guard vessel Simcoe to the Port Weller yard now.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EFFECT ON WESTERN ECONOMY
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EFFECT ON WESTERN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canada-U.S. trade agreement is good news for Saskatchewan and the West. The agreement takes an important step toward ending the insane global grain wars as both countries seek a level playing field in North American grain subsidies and work together in global negotiations.
Red meat producers will gain exemption from U.S. meat import laws. Canadian cattlemen will no longer be blind-sided by American disputes with third countries.
The agreement will end the protectionist threat against our energy exports. Exciting new opportunities will be created for western development in oil, natural gas, hydro, and uranium. Reduced tariffs will cause consumer prices to fall. Our production costs will be lower, and our ability to add value will be improved-a key factor in western diversification.
Our future lies in the prosperity of free trade, not in the poverty of protectionism. Consumers, energy producers, grain farmers, cattlemen and pork producers all stand to gain through this historic initiative.

ELIGIBILITY FOR DISABILITY BENEFIT-WIDER DISTRIBUTION OF INFORMATION URGED

Mr. Speaker, many Canadians are not aware of the stringent requirements that have to be met in order to qualify for a disability benefit under the Canada Pension Plan. In fact, the applicant has to be practically comatose to become eligible. Once total disability has been proven, the next obstacle to be overcome is the earnings contribution formula.

The valiant revolution began on October 23, 1956, and for a brief moment in history the Hungarian people won their

October 23, 1987

freedom and independence. Factory workers and students joined together to demand the withdrawal of Soviet troops from their country. The demonstrations were, at first, peaceful. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Deputy Prime Minister I will direct my question to the Minister of Finance. It is with regard to the
free trade agreement. On October 5, the day the agreement was tabled in the House of Commons, the Minister of Agriculture was commenting on the U.S. subsidies and grain wars. He said:

Enhancement Program into our traditional markets.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of State and Minister of State (Treasury Board)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF ORGANIZATIONS FOUNDATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my honour and privilege to make a statement on the occasion of United Nations Day.
Tomorrow will once again mark United Nations Day. On that day, 42 years ago, amid the chaos and violence of war, the United Nations was founded. It is reassuring to contemplate both the conditions under which this world body was born and the purpose for which it was created.
If today we are sometimes disturbed and discouraged over the seeming intractable and persistent problems facing the world community, let us take heart and renewed courage and determination to persist in making the world a better place to live. Let us recall that a commitment to a strong United Nations, and to its programs, offers one of the enduring hopes for the betterment of the human condition.

Madam Speaker, Canada is pursuing its efforts to strengthen the structure of the United Nations. To that end, it is working from the inside, with energy and perseverance, to ensure that reforms improve the effectiveness and efficiency of UN operations and administration. By acting on its principles, for instance by forgiving the debts of Third World nations faced with serious financial problems and by continuing to make a major financial contribution to the UN, Canada reflects the convictions of Canadians. In fact, Canadians believe that the best way to promote peace and justice in through fair economic development, that the struggle for justice and human rights is a cause that deserves material support and that all nations should share both the benefits of development and the burden of poverty.

Canadians, of all people, recognize that we are very much dependent on the health of the international community. United Nations Day should serve, therefore, to remind us afresh of our commitment to responsible and responsive internationalism and to the ideals of the United Nations Charter.

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF ORGANIZATIONS FOUNDATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians know and support the United Nations. Many Canadians, both English-speaking and French-speaking, have served with organizations that are part of United Nations, inspired by the ideals and goals set down in the Charter forty-two years ago. Many Canadians have served in UN peacekeeping forces throughout the world, and Canadian lives have been lost for the sake of world peace. Today-

All nations of the world look to the United Nations for leadership, maintaining peace and ensuring development while
protecting the environment. Peace, development and the environment are the magnets which today attract nations to the United Nations with the same intensity as did the ideal of peace in 1945. However, the United Nations can only be as strong as the political will of each member nation.
It would be a mistake to believe that the United Nations can impose its will on the world. It cannot. The speed with which the United Nations can proceed depends on the speed of its member nations. Therefore, it is important for Canada to ensure that our enthusiasm for the United Nations is shared by nations whose reluctance these days slows down the implementation of the United Nations' over-all mandate.
In 1952, a distinguished Canadian, Lester B. Pearson, became President of the General Assembly. Canadians take great pride in the contribution he made and the legacy he left. It is interesting to note that in his book Peace in the Family of Man, Lester B. Pearson concluded with these words:
People-must be made to see that internationalism is quite as important to them, as practically and immediately important, as national loyalty and interest; important not merely in an academic and remote or idealistic sense, but important as something which immediately and concretely affects their well-being, their very lives.
We must apply the science and art of politics to the affairs of the international community with the intensity of personal involvement that we give to domestic affairs.
Mr. Pearson's words were as true then as they are today as we once again celebrate United Nations Day.

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF ORGANIZATIONS FOUNDATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am honoured to speak for my Party in recognizing the achievements and goals of the United Nations which was founded in 1945 to end the scourge of war. Since that time its achievements have been many. Canadians want to defend and strengthen the United Nations and we take a critical view of those who undermine its legitimacy or its relevance.
In 1985, when polled on the question, "How important do you think it is that we try to make the United Nations a success?", 83 per cent of Canadians said it is important or very important.
Disappointment with the United Nations should be addressed to the lack of commitment and co-operation among member states rather than faulting the international institution itself. The Soviet Union should be commended for recently paying all its outstanding debts to the United Nations, especially those for the peacekeeping missions it had long refused to support. No nation should withhold funds because decisions taken collectively go against its particular viewpoint. We hope the example of the Soviet initiative will not be lost on the United States.
Global interdependency has increased since the founding of the United Nations, as have the complexity of the problems facing human kind, including the threat of nuclear weapons, poverty, underdevelopment, human rights abuse, malnutrition and environmental degradation. No nation can solve these
October 23, 1987

problems alone. Now is not the time to abandon the United Nations' system. Collective co-operation is needed to ease the Third World debt crisis, to end the Iran-Iraq war, to end apartheid in South Africa and to defend the delicate balance of the Guatemala peace accord.
Canadians can be proud of our contribution to the United Nations. We have participated in more observer groups and peace-keeping missions than any other member state. Numerous Canadians have distinguished themselves in service to the United Nations and its agencies.
Recently, our mission led the drive to strengthen the role and involvement of women within the United Nations, and a Canadian woman, Madam Therese Paquet-Sevigny, has become the first woman to be named Under-Secretary General.
Canada is respected as a middle power and is in a favourable position to steer a sane course between the posturing rivalry of the superpowers. Above all, we can support the process of replacing dependency with interdependency, particularly where the poorer countries strive to defend their interests on an equal footing with rich, developed countries.
I would like to take this occasion to commend the work of the United Nations Association in Canada for its perseverance, hard work and educational activities to inform Canadians about the United Nations. Canadians should know that the United Nations is our institution, for behind the United Nations, as the Secretary General has said, "stands the single, collective constituency of the human race, a vast silent majority which wants peace with justice and dignity, with freedom from fear and want and the hope of a better tomorrow".

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. McMillan that Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Madam Speaker, when 1 terminated my remarks just prior to the beginning of Statements by Members at eleven o'clock, I was dealing with the point of one of the requested inclusions in an environmental Bill of rights, namely, standing and access to the courts.
I was pointing out to Hon. Members that this is a right already enjoyed by Canadians. Private individuals have the right to prosecute federal summary conviction offences. They also have the same right for indictable offences, only, of course, with the permission of the court. In both instances it is possible for provincial Attorneys General to step in and assume the prosecution.
This power to intervene is specifically dealt with in the Criminal Code and pertains to all federal offences, not just those found in the Bill before us this morning. The power of the Attorneys General to intervene is fundamental to the administration of justice in Canada. This authority should not be dealt with, I would suggest, in an ad hoc manner by attempts to change it through the Canadian environmental protection Bill.
Involvement by the public in federal decision making is already possible in the development of regulations. This has been true, I guess, since the beginning of our Confederation in the normal call for comments when proposed regulations are published in The Canada Gazette in Part I.
The role of the public has been further guaranteed by the Government in its March, 1986, citizen's code of regulatory fairness. This is a very important development, which I do not think has received the attention that it deserves from the Canadian public. I understand that it has been the practice of Environment Canada in its policy to have public consultation on regulatory matters, even prior to the existence of this code to which I just referred. Therefore, citizens can already exercise powers under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. Their role in enforcement will be larger now than ever before under any other federal statute.
Over the past days of this debate, several of my colleagues have stated and reiterated the vital role that this Bill will play in the task of protecting our environment. We have underscored the methods proposed to attack the problem head on. We all concur that the responsibilities rest with each one of us to ensure a healthy environment for our children and for our children's children. However, the responsibility at present rests with this House to get on with the passage of this Bill. I propose that we do just that.
I look forward to a more detailed debate of the Bill once it gets to committee. Therefore, it is not my intention to prolong this stage of the Bill.

I wish to ask the Hon. Member a question on the environmental bill of rights. The Hon. Member made reference to the concept, and seems to be under the mistaken impression that there is in effect an environmental bill of rights in this Bill before us today. That is not the case, and it has been a major criticism on the part of environmental groups and experts in the country.
Earlier in his speech, the Hon. Member referred to consultation and he pointed out that there would be consultation with the provinces. Certainly, I would heartily agree that there ought to be consultation with the provinces, although not a lessening of standards for the environment on the part of the provinces. The provinces ought to have the right to increase standards but not to decrease them.
October 23, 1987

The Hon. Member did not mention, apropos consultation, consultation with environmentalist groups. Those groups were very much excluded from the process. The Bill was expanded rather after the fact that a consultation had taken place on only a part of the Bill. They feel that they have been excluded from this process. They have asked the Government to pass this Bill, get on with things, but to go back to square one, as it were, to meet with them and come up with a real environmental bill of rights that will do the types of things that they have been asking to be done over the last number of years.

I thank the Hon. Member for her question. I do not think 1 indicated in my remarks that there was an environmental bill of rights contained in this statute. I pointed out that there perhaps is what is tantamount to that in there, in that there is ample opportunity for citizen participation in the investigation process, and in the research process. I suggest that the Hon. Member examine the sections, from Section 100 on, which deal with the investigation, some of which I referred to in my remarks, such as the opportunity for any 12 persons to petition the Minister to investigate an alleged offence.
In terms of the comments of the Hon. Member on consultation, up until now it has been my understanding that there has been significant consultation by the Department and the Minister during the last several months with environmental groups, certainly with the provinces, and with companies that will be involved. I would suggest that it is the type of consultation that must occur in any democratic confederation such as ours. I think that it has occurred in this case. Perhaps there is room for more consultation and discussions. I am sure that the Minister will be prepared to talk and continue to talk to people. Certainly, there will be a monitoring of the legislation once it is in force to ensure that it is meeting the requirements of all Canadians.
As I suggested in my remarks, it is an important step forward. It is the type of legislation that will give us the instrument to deal with our commitments internationally, and our genuine commitment that was underlined this week at the United Nations General Assembly by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) to give effect to the Brundtland report, that important study and commission which recognizes, as does this Act, the important connection between the environment and the economy.
It is those types of provisions contained in the Bill before the House which will give the Government, in conjunction with other Governments of the country and citizens, the right to take part in developing the type of interaction that has to occur if we are to deal with the serious environmental problems that will face us in the future.
In closing, one such example is the ozone treaty. It is an extremely important historical development in terms of environmental protection. The meetings took place in Montreal under the leadership of the Government and the Minister of the Environment. We need this Bill to be enacted in order to give effect to our commitments under that treaty.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a few comments on the principles involved in Bill C-74, and on where it falls short, in my opinion.
We must realize at the beginning that when we are talking about the environment and we look at specific examples that are site-specific we are talking about a global problem. Whether we are talking about Ladysmith Harbour, Cowichan Estuary, something to do with the Love Canal, or low-level flights in Labrador, we are talking about a global problem.
I have a great deal of concern that our parliamentary system is not addressing that global problem in the global context. When I say "our parliamentary system" I do not only mean the Canadian parliamentary system, I mean parliamentary systems all over the world. Parliamentary democracy is the best hope that people of our world have that there will be an intelligent approach to environmental problems. Certainly dictatorships have done an even worse job of addressing the environment than parliamentary democracies.
This is something that we collectively as a House of Commons have to address; the fact that environmental problems in our world are outstripping our ability to control them and deal with them in a constructive manner. We live in a world where there are 5 billion people. That population is growing, yet the resources on which those 5 billion people depend are finite.
The Brundtland report which was released this past spring points to the very real problems that we have, and that we in the developed world sometimes ignore. Because we are able to exploit resources that are a thousand miles away from us and the degradation is sometimes hidden from our eyes, we neglect to see what really is happening in the world.
The Brundtland report makes the basic observation that we cannot continue to have the type of anti-environmental policies in the developed world that lead to underdevelopment and poverty in the Third World, and hope that this will be sustainable in the medium-level or long-term future. The future of our world depends upon finding models of development that can be applied throughout our world, not only in the industrialized West, but in the Third World, that will enable all people to live together with some dignity and prosperity.
The types of pressures that the developed world places on the environment are different from the types of pressures placed on the environment in the Third World. For example, I can remember when the external affairs committee visited Tanzania, and drove through the countryside and saw stacks of charcoal by the side of the road. This charcoal was made by chopping down the local forests. It was sent into the City of Dar es Salaam to provide much needed fuel for heating and cooking. It was a source of energy. Yet that source of energy was directly responsible for destroying forests. The destruction of forests in our world is a shame and a crisis that will affect all of us in a very short time unless we find some way of addressing it.

October 23, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
The Brundtland report pointed out that already we are beginning to experience some of the problems that we have inflicted upon our world. They are coming back to haunt us. There was the African famine of three or four years ago. Now there are reports that we again have drought in Ethiopia and millions of people's lives are at risk. This is not simply a cyclical matter of drought in the sub-Sahara area. There have been cyclical droughts, certainly. It is also a result of the fact that we have abused the environment. For example, 45 per cent of Ethiopia used to be covered by forests. Today about 4 per cent is covered by forests. This kind of human abuse of the environment is causing many of our problems.
We have seen the effects of the Chernobyl nuclear disaster and the Bhopol chemical disaster in India. In Canada a couple of years ago a Senate study talked about the growing problem of the destruction of our land, the salinization of Canadian land. We are concerned about the disappearance of whole species of animal and plant life.
Recently a number of us from our Party, and I think from other Parties, wrote to the chairman of the World Bank, Barber Conable, and urged that the World Bank's development policies should take much greater cognizance of the need for environmental protection to be built into every project undertaken by the World Bank. Sometimes World Bank projects have been very short sighted where dams have been built and areas flooded with no consequence to the total environment in which the dam has been placed. Instead of having positive development, we end up with another environmental disaster.
The Brundtland report suggested having a United Nations declaration on the environment, similar to the United Nations declaration of human rights that has become a standard through which people from all over the world can appeal. We should have that kind of universal standard for the environment.
This is not simply a Canadian problem or a problem in Tanzania, India or wherever, it is a global problem. We all share it and we should be working to develop a United Nations approach to this. This is particularly appropriate now with United Nations Day falling tomorrow.
In the same respect, it has been urged that Canada itself should adopt an environmental bill of rights which would guarantee to the Canadian people certain environmental standards. The Government gave some lip service to this concept, but Bill C-74 does not begin to address the need for an environmental bill of rights. It adds a preamble which has some very laudable wording and goals in it, but it does not have any effect in law.
Let me point to some of the things it says:
WHEREAS the presence of toxic substances in the environment is a matter of national concern;
WHEREAS toxic substances once introduced into the environment cannot always be contained within geographic boundaries;
WHEREAS the Government of Canada in demonstrating national leadership should establish national environmental quality objectives, guidelines and codes of practice;
WHEREAS it is necessary to control the dispersal of nutrients in Canadian waters;
WHEREAS some of the laws under which federal lands, works and undertakings are administered or regulated do not make provision for environmental protection in respect to federal lands and undertakings;
AND WHEREAS Canada must be able to fulfil its international obligations in respect of the environment;
The preamble concludes that therefore the Government passes the following law and so on. What we would like to see is a basic declaration of rights of Canadians as far as the environment is concerned. Perhaps we can get a better idea of some of the problems with Bill C-74. We support it as a small step forward, but it is not the kind of Environment Protection Act that Canadians really need. I would like to give an example.
A couple of weekends ago I had the opportunity to take a trip through the Cowichan Estuary and up the river. We were concerned about the low water levels on the Cowichan River because the levels affect the salmon. The mill was closed. It was a Saturday morning and all was very quiet and peaceful. The colours were changing in the mountains and it was a very beautiful scene. We saw fish and seals eating the fish. There were ducks and hunters were out trying to shoot the ducks. As we went up the river we saw some Indian people spearing fish and then we saw a great blue heron which flew out from the trees on the edge of the river and glided across the river. The blue heron is a magnificent and beautiful bird, Madam Speaker.
Just a few miles north of the Cowichan River at Crofton a colony of blue herons with 57 nests were counted last year but not one egg hatched from those nests. Canadian wildlife officials have been sampling eggs from the blue heron colonies in four specific locations in British Columbia over the past number of years and have found dioxin levels in three of the samples. The highest level has been at the Crofton area. Not one of those eggs in the 57 nests hatched this past year.
This is a kind of mini-environmental disaster for that particular colony of great blue herons. It has frightening implications for all of us because blue herons happen to be at the top end of the food chain. They tend to live on fish and sea creatures which themselves will ingest minute quantities of dioxins. Blue herons at the top of the food chain are more subject to the problems of dioxins than animals lower in the food chain.
There has been a lot of circumstantial evidence about why none of the 57 nests produced a single hatched egg, and it looks as though the problem is related to dioxins. We are not completely sure what the source is, whether it is from the Crofton pulp mill which employs a good number of people in my constituency and is extremely important to the economy of
October 23, 1987

that area, or whether it could from the kind of wood preservative used by the local sawmills. Does it come through ingestion of fish or shellfish? Some of the preliminary testing has not shown very high levels of dioxins in local fish, but we have asked that the fisheries people do more testing to determine the problem. There is some question about the use of shellfish in that area. The contamination of the whole British Columbia coast poses a threat to human beings. There has been a much higher percentage of dioxins found in British Columbia than anywhere else in Canada. The great blue herons are used as a kind of thermometer for registering dioxins and it has been shown that they are under much greater stress in British Columbia. Some of the colonies appear to have moved away from the coast where we have a large number of our pulp mills. The total population of great blue herons is probably diminishing on our coast. That says something about the degradation of the environment which has very important implications for human beings.
The question we need to ask is how would Bill C-74 make a difference to that situation. If the route of the dioxins to the blue herons was from a sawmill or a pulp mill using PCBs or wood preservatives to the fish or shellfish and then to the blue herons, then Bill C-74 would make no difference at all, because Clause 38(2)(b) of the Bill provides that the Minister can act only if he has consulted with other Ministers of the Crown in right of Canada to determine whether any action can be taken under any other Act of Parliament to prevent the significant danger referred to in subclause 1.
The Fisheries Act gives the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon) the power to control deleterious substances which affect fish habitat or fish, so the authority is already there. Bill C-74 will not provide any further protection to solve that particular problem if in fact the pattern of dioxins had been from an industrial plant to fish and then to the blue herons.
If some other route was followed, the Minister of the Environment could place the discharges that were responsible for the dioxin level on a list of substances to be regulated, but this is a lengthy and cumbersome process. There is no simple answer.
Pesticide regulation rests with Agriculture Canada and it has input from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and from Environment Canada. Fisheries and Oceans and Environment Canada have jurisdiction over water quality as it affects fish, and there are sometimes little jurisdictional jealousies among people who work in those different departments. This Bill does not clear up that jurisdictional jealousy.
As I said, we have not established conclusively that heron eggs suffer from dioxin levels. If they do, the source could either be pulp mill effluent or wood preservatives used on lumber. The blame is tossed back and forth from one industry to another.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Environment Canada is looking at PCBs used in wood preservatives as a priority chemical to be controlled in spite of the fact that Agriculture Canada has registered that chemical, and it has since backed off. Under Bill C-74, if PCBs become a priority substance they will be tested and regulations will be drawn up which will be subject to review by a board which will include industry. Once passed, it would restrict the chemical.
One official from Environment Canada told my office that this is a process measured in years. This brings me back to the initial comment I made, is that our parliamentary system seems to be so slow in dealing with the mounting environmental crisis that the crisis is outstripping our ability to deal with it. Certainly the process envisaged in Bill C-74 moves very slowly.
The Environmental Contaminants Act, which Bill C-74 would replace, deals with new chemicals excluding pesticides and existing chemicals but does not apply to chemicals covered by other Acts. The pressure to put PCBs on the priority list to be examined by Environment Canada is being resisted. The province is saying that ten parts per million is considered by the industry to be a very onerous restriction. The chemical that is being developed to replace PCBs will have a lower acceptable level of five parts per million because it is more acutely toxic to fish, but there is less information to suggest that it is a chronic health hazard. We are replacing one group of chemicals with another which we hope will be less hazardous to our health, even though we know that it is more toxic to fish.
There is a whole host of areas where the Government now has the power to act. It has the power to act under the Fisheries Act, for example, but it has not acted. For example, the Fraser River as it flows into the ocean becomes practically a sewer for different kinds of chemical wastes, but the Department of Fisheries has not acted to clean up the mess. Bill C-74 will not help that situation. Ladysmith Harbour has a long-standing problem and Bill C-74 will not solve that because the Government already has legislation in place and Bill C-74 will not infringe on that legislation.
Therefore, while we support this legislation as a small step, it does not begin to address the fundamental problems of the environment in Canada or the world as they exist in 1987.

I think it is important for the people watching to have some perspective on just how important a report this is and how this Government has recognized that and acted in a very significant way to respond to it.
First, before it handed down its report, when the commission visited Canada in the spring of 1986, the Minister of the

Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Environment made a presentation to it. Subsequent to that, a task force on the environment and the economy was established by the Minister consisting of Government, industry and environmental groups. Madam Speaker, certainly I would want to commend the Minister for his personal commitment to the environment and I think it is highly commendable that he did go to the United Nations to raise this. I think it has to be raised in a great number of forums. I appreciate, and I think Canadians appreciate that he went to the United Nations to raise it because I think it is important.
I am also concerned about the lag time. The Minister spoke about the slowness with which we are dealing with this Bill. We have no intention of holding it up, but I am concerned that the Bill itself move slowly in order to address the problems of our environment. It is a very small step to deal with a very serious problem. We, like the Hon. Member, want to see it move forward, but it is important that Canadians understand from this debate that it does not begin to give the kind of total protection of the environment that its title somewhat grandiosely suggests.
