Madam Speaker, at the outset I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Cowichan- Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) for his endorsement of the efforts of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) to represent environmental issues for Canada. The original suggestion that the stature of the Minister is international in scope is of course based upon his efforts to address
not only Canada's environmental problems but global environmental problems. To the degree to which his Government allowed him, I think the former Minister of the Environment, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), also enjoyed international stature in the environmental sense. However, what has occurred since then with our Government has been a quantum leap forward. I disagree with my friend from Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands. This is not a small step forward. It is a very major step forward. Until now there has been no way in which the Government through legislation could truly track the life-span of new and existing chemicals and their interaction with the environment, whether it be plant life, the air, animals, birds, or human beings.
I have had an ongoing interest in environmental issues going back to 1974. For example, I can recall in the mid-1970s when the Government of Canada, and the then Minister of National Health and Welfare, Marc Lalonde, were persuaded to fund a study into the effects of lead fall-out on the residents of Trail and greater Trail. That was instigated by studies which determined that some horses, particularly foals, were affected in their bone structure and general health by lead poisoning. There are those of us familiar with the effect that that has on bone and soft tissue. However, half-way through the study the Government decided not to fund it any longer. It was through my efforts, supported by Local 480 of the Steelworkers Union and Dr. Smith, the public health officer, that Marc Lalonde, who is difficult to persuade at any time, was persuaded to complete this important study.
I recall seeing patients in my office, workers at the smelter, who suffered erosion of their teeth because of acid in the air in the zinc plant. I saw people with a hole through the nasal septum big enough to put a gold ring through as a result of tissue erosion. I can say now that were it not for the forceful actions of Local 480, those working conditions would not have been improved. They have a continuous and ongoing concern about those working conditions.
I have a constituent who is a victim of paint spray in a body shop he owns. We cannot even find out what the chemistry is that is causing the problem because the company producing the paint does not want to tell us. Yet he has respiratory involvement, circulatory involvement, dermatitis, psychological impact, and all kinds of other sensitivities which he never had before. He has lost the ability to work in his profession in his body shop, and he is a very skilled tradesman.
It was I think a year ago that we saw on television prairie farmers suffering nausea, vomiting, dermatitis, and vertigo as a result of the inhalation of fumes from herbicides or pesticides sprayed on their farmland. There is concern that this Bill does not address that problem. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney), in his speech which began yesterday and finished today dealt with that very appropriately. Those concerns should not be concerns of major importance to the public.
October 23, 1987

In speaking to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King), I reflected upon the problems created for fruit farmers in spraying their trees. The ignorance displayed in not using a face mask when spraying fruit trees, for example, resulted in death in one case. The same concerns can be raised over the life span and effect of other chemicals. Certainly a significant group of my constituents have been very concerned about the application of herbicides and pesticides by the B.C. Forest Service, CP Rail, Burlington Rail, and the Department of Highways. Many of them appear to have a better knowledge of the chemistry involved than the provincial Departments we are dealing with.
It is important to all of us that we get a handle on this. It is in that context that this Bill addresses such a multitude of subjects. It is a Bill of such scope and dimension that I do not think any of us truly appreciate it at this stage. To address the concerns expressed by the Hon. Member for Cowichan- Malahat-The Islands, who says that changes should be made to the Bill, there needs to be more improvement, I say that may be that is so, but we will have that opportunity in committee. I hope this Bill will be before that committee very shortly.
The magnitude of environmental issues today boggles the mind. If it were not for the fact that life in Canada north of the 49th parallel was very hard in the days of the pioneers, I think some of us would wish we could go back to that time and start all over again with the knowledge we have now of the environmental impact of the things we do. However, that is not to be, so we must endeavour with great energy to reverse that process.
Reference was made to the blue heron. Not too long ago this Government funded in part an experimental boiler for a pulp mill in my constituency. We put $380,000 into a project that will cost approximately $1.5 to $2 million. When that boiler is in place the pulp mill will experience a reduction of about 90 per cent in both water-borne and airborne pollutants. That is Canadian technology at work in concert with other pulp and paper companies across Canada, and the Province of British Columbia. If that technology works, and we have every reason to believe it will, it will generate jobs in a market which is just waiting for that Canadian technology.
There are at least 40 different locations right now in Canada where that technology can be applied. There are about 80 or more in the United States. There are about 400 known applications worldwide right now. That technology originated in Canada. In fact, the first model which originated in my constituency will, in my view, make a very significant contribution to the reduction of air and water-borne pollutants coming from pulp mills.
I would like to correct the Hon. Member in one context. He made reference to pulp mills using wood preservatives. It would be the first time, to my knowledge, that they have
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
resorted to that. I cannot understand why wood preservatives would ever be used in a pulp mill. They never made that reference with regard to dioxins and other products which are contained in some wood preservatives.
Major contribution to the environment has been made by the Minister of the Environment. He and the Member for Davenport, when he was the Minister, gained international stature. Canada has been recognized at the table of the United Nations and is in the forefront on concerns for the environment. I thank God for that.
There are no simple answers. This is a very complex subject ranging from dioxin to the ozone layer to the food chain and to a host of new chemistry about which we do not, as yet, know a thing. All of those will require the very close scrutiny of the Government of Canada through this Act, the Fisheries Act, pesticide control by the Department of Agriculture, and the Ocean Dumping Control Act.
My colleague from Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands expressed concern that this issue was not addressed in this Bill, but it was addressed in another Bill. Frankly, I see no reason why, if ocean dumping is well addressed in the Ocean Dumping Control Act, it should be moved into the Environmental Protection Act. That would only expand the debate and delay the Bill further. The same would apply to the Fisheries Act. We need not take portions out of that Act and put it in this Bill.
This is a very comprehensive Bill which will, in my view, move Canada forward in its concern for the environment. It is not the final answer. We do not yet know what is out there. The Minister would be the first to admit that this is not the final answer, but it is a quantum leap forward and a contribution and example to the world.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to contribute to this debate although this is not a subject on which I profess any wide knowledge, certainly not worldwide knowledge such as some others have, including my colleague, the Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly). However, I am concerned with this subject and the way in which it has affected the residents of Spadina and another part of Toronto for some years.
In 1972 I became aware that a lead smelter a few blocks from my house was polluting the neighbourhood. The lead smelter had grown up from a scrap-yard which had concentrated on smelting lead. I was very interested in the remarks of the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) who described dealing with a very similar problem at Trail in conjunction with Steel Workers' Local 480. I commend the Hon. Member for his part in the work that was done there. I commend the steel workers for their part in it as well.
I will describe a little of the difficulty that we had in approaching this problem. I was then the alderman for the ward concerned. The company concerned was Toronto Refiners and Smelters at the corner of Bathurst and Front

October 23, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Streets. Within a year or so another company, Canada Metals, owned by the same outfit which owned the Trail smelter, Canada Pacific Investments, was causing the same problem two or three miles east at the foot of Pape Avenue.
We lacked almost entirely the legal tools needed to deal with that problem. We could not get action directly from the provincial Government, which at that time had jurisdiction over air quality. We had to use the local board of health. The local board of health, of course, has some very peremptory powers, but mostly on a different scale. It gives the medical officer of health power to order the repair or replacement of a faulty sanitary toilet if it is causing trouble to the neighbours. That does not go very far toward correcting a problem with a smelter.
When we directed the company, through the board of health, to stop spewing lead dust on to the neighbouring streets and houses in which people had been living before the plant was established, we were met with massive legal action. We were met with costs in the range of $100,000. Fortunately, the provincial Government allowed city council to reimburse three members of the board of health who were specifically acted against in a civil suit by a combination of the lead companies.
We learned that there is an international lead-zinc research organization which sends specialists throughout the world to testify, where necessary, that a little bit of lead does not really hurt you and to try to overshadow any local experts who may be able to show that there has been or is likely to be a harmful effect from the ingestion of lead, especially in children of preschool age.
We were finally able to make enough public fuss that the provincial Ministry of the Environment was pressured to take action in the matter. After several years it issued control orders requiring the companies to clean up to some extent. The problem has not been very well monitored and the pollution has continued, not at the same rate, but at a rate serious enough to require the replacement of the soil for the second time. Soil was replaced on the orders of the provincial Government because it was unfit to be on the property of families, especially those with small children. That was done at public expense rather than the expense of the company. The evidence now shows that the soil in some of those areas has been polluted a second time. Even though there was provincial legislation, the control has been very weak.
There was also a labour problem. Upon inquiry we found that in at least one plant workers who were tested by the company doctor for lead content in their blood were told not to worry, that they were okay. Not every family doctor has the knowledge or equipment to test for small quantities of lead in the blood. Therefore, we had some of them tested elsewhere, and the level of lead content found in their blood was medically shocking. They were shocked. They were quite unhappy at the thought that the company-paid doctor misled them. The fact is that the philosophy of the company doctor is that the patient is the company since it pays his bills. Therefore, he will
give the workers such information as the company wishes him to give them.
The workers in the plant found that not only was the neighbourhood being polluted, their health and lives were being endangered by lead. At that time we could find no help from the federal Government. However, I want to say, to the credit of the Speaker of the House, that in 1979 he was the Minister of the Environment and, in correspondence with me, indicated that he hoped to introduce a law that would enable the federal Government to take some action in cases like that. He was unable to finish that project.
Thanks to you guys.

I hear an Hon. Member say thanks to us. I was not here then but I understand that the Hon. Member's Party produced a foolish budget and did not even make sure they had enough people in the House to support it. They are still kicking themselves for that, but do not like to admit who really was at fault.
However, I wish to commend the Speaker, the then Minister, for at least attempting to take action on this.
This law is at least a beginning, part of which is to identify toxic substances. However, there are some problems with that aspect, as with others.
Labour groups and other environmentally concerned groups who appeared before the committee pointed out that the definition of a toxic substance, while very wide in one sense, is very weak in another sense.
It states:
For the purposes of this Part, a substance is toxic if it is entering or may enter the environment in a quantity or concentration or under conditions
(a)	having or that may have a significant immediate or long-term harmful effect on the environment that is likely to interfere with important biological processes;
(b)	constituting or that may constitute a danger to the environment on which human life depends; or
(c)	constituting or that may constitute a danger in Canada to human life or health.
That is a very broad definition. The problem is that it is also very vague. The Government may or may not declare a substance to be toxic. There is not much provision in the act to reassure the public that the Government will act on that matter. I will deal with that question in more detail later.
A further problem is that the arrangement between the federal Government and provincial Governments seems quite unsatisfactory because it allows for indefinite waffling between Ottawa and one or more provincial capitals. It allows for an indefinite period of consultation, before which the Government may not act.
One can envisage Ottawa blaming a province and a province blaming Ottawa, each one saying the other is not moving. This
October 23, 1987

is very unsatisfactory from the point of view of the public who would like to see some action. The Bill does not prevent the Government from acting, by law, but allows for passing the buck between the federal Government and the provinces, as in university funding, for example. The federal Government and the Ontario Government blame each other for the fact that universities are short of funds. The same danger can exist with this legislation. The Government will not want to put the funds into the work, and therefore leave it to the provincial Government, which will say that this is a federal responsibility.
Furthermore, according to Clause 38(2), there must even be a consultation before an emergency order can be issued. We had this experience in trying to get an emergency order to clean up or temporarily close in order to clean up these lead smelters in Toronto. The local board of health did not have sufficient legal clout to do that. In effect, the legislation was not strong enough. I do not know whether the provincial legislation was strong enough or whether there was simply a lack of will on the part of the provincial Government since it took so long to take action.
There is some risk in this case that the federal Government will simply delay while consulting with a provincial Government even on an emergency order.
Let me turn to the general problem of the need for minimum legislation. The Canadian Labour Congress stated:
The general principle ought to be: Unless the provinces have stronger legislation, the federal Government should move in to establish minimum-but strong and effective-national standards of environmental cleanliness.
There should be consultation with the interested parties, certainly; but this should not prevent speedy and effective federal Government action on the environment at the national level.
In other words, there should not be so much buck-passing with respect to emergency orders and particularly legislation. There should be a clearly established federal responsibility for a minimum standard. There is nothing stopping a province from implementing a higher standard, but it should not be allowed to tolerate a lower standard.
Many people have often spoken about the need for a bill of environmental rights. While it is true that there is the right of 12 people to petition the Minister for information for an investigation, it does not give them the right to initiate any kind of civil action. That is a very serious defect in this Bill. Unless they are prepared to show that individually they are being harmed or likely to be harmed, they cannot use Clause 128 and Clause 129 to initiate civil action. While they can use Clauses 100 and 101 to get information, it can be a very slow process, and it is unclear whether they will be able to initiate actions after they have the information.
Of course, there is no provision for funding such an action. As I said, companies like Canadian Pacific Investment, which are in the business of polluting, can spend millions of dollars on their international lead and zinc research outfit in order to combat anyone, such as workers in the plant, neighbours down the street, or even people in the community who may be trying
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
to get the information and lay a charge under civil action but do not have an expensive researcher on retainer. In such cases, it will be a contest of the elephant against the mouse.
It is the same in the matter of determining what is toxic and what is non-toxic. Yes, 12 persons may be able to petition to have the Minister investigate a certain substance to see whether or not it is toxic, but they will not have the right to initiate civil action in the matter. Therefore, while the Government is acquiring information, and that is good, and of course it is necessary to have the information, the likelihood of corrective action is in great doubt. In spite of public requests at the hearings in this matter, the opportunities for the public to secure corrective action are very limited.
Finally, I wish to refer to one large omission under this Act. There are others, but the one with which I am very concerned is its neglect to deal with environmental dangers of nuclear energy and radio-active substances. It is also a matter dealt with not in my ward but within Metro Toronto, when previous Governments, federal and provincial, left radio-active soil in a dump in Scarborough without even informing subsequent developers and homeowners of what might be in that soil. They found out later on, after the homes had been bought and the owners had begun to live in them, that they were living on a radio-active dump. It has taken years of expensive and tortuous litigation for those homeowners to get some satisfaction from one or the other levels of government.
Apparently this law does nothing at all to correct that defect. We may be told that that is all taken care of by the Atomic Energy Control Board. If so, that is a sick joke, because, as we found out when the new appointments were being made about a year ago, almost all of the members of that board were engaged in making profits, or else they come immediately from companies which are engaged in making profits out of the atomic energy business. That is putting the fox in charge of the chicken coop. Those men are not going to restrict their profits by having concern for the health and safety of the people in the neighbourhood or the countryside around them.
Therefore, we have neither under the atomic energy legislation, nor in this EPA, any serious means by which the public can ensure protection for itself against mistakes, excesses or negligence on the part of those who conduct our nuclear energy plants and industries, and the transportation of toxic substances which sometimes travel on a railway line through Metro Toronto, and so on. None of that is under sufficient control. It is unfortunate that that aspect has been omitted from this Act.
As I said, my colleagues and I are supporting this Act. I am specifically thankful that some steps have been taken, because I know the problem we had a decade ago in Toronto, and still have. I regret the Act is so cautious and particularly so afraid

Canadian Environmental Protection Act
of allowing the public full modern necessary access to the remedies concerned.

Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the speech of the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) who, as usual, has thoroughly examined the matter before us. I did not hear him comment, however, on one aspect of the Bill which might interest him and on which I would seek his views. The Hon. Member is probably not aware of the fact that in Bill C-74 there is a clause which does not empower the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) to stop the export of substances that are prohibited for use in Canada, but which Canada may want to export, for instance, to developing countries for economic, commercial and other reasons.
This, of course, raises a moral question which I am sure the Hon. Member for Spadina is particularly keen and qualified to examine, namely, whether Canada should be engaged in the export of substances, in this case it would be toxic substances, that we do not permit for use in our own jurisdiction, but for which we would not have any compunction at all to seek to have exported.
1 must admit that I could not understand the reasoning of the Government in not including a clause to the effect that the Minister would have the power to stop exports of substances of this kind once they are forbidden for use here. Evidently, the political will was not sufficient in Cabinet and, therefore, we have to address the question here at second reading and subsequently in committee.
It is with this thought in mind that I would invite the Hon. Member for Spadina to give us the benefit of his reflection on this clause as he assesses it from a moral point of view.

Madam Speaker, 1 thank the Hon. Member for his comment. 1 am aware of the defect he mentions, and there are many defects in the Bill I did not have time to touch upon, and I agree that it is a serious defect. I cannot match the Hon. Member's expertise on the subject, but I heartily agree with the principle to which he has appealed, that if a substance is too poisonous to use for Canadians, it is too poisonous to use in anyone else's country.
It is a disgrace that we should knowingly permit the export to other countries, as the Hon. Member says, probably to third world or what 1 would call "former colonial countries"-more colonial than Canada-those people who are in a sense economically weaker, of substances which perhaps some Canadian company wishes to sell to its profit or wishes to use in a subsidiary in that other country, notwithstanding the fact that it is likely to do harm to those people such as might be prohibited by law to be done to Canadians.
This is, of course, part and parcel of the growing practice of multinational corporations which are seeking to shut down industries in Canada so they can open them up in former colonial countries that lack even such protections as we have here for the environment, for the conditions of labour and, of course, for the wages of labour.
When I was in El Salvador, I was invited by the Vice Minister of Planning to encourage Canadians to invest in what he called "our low wages, our low-wage industries", and I am quite sure that any Canadian who wished to export a manufacturing enterprise to El Salvador and wished to use toxic substances, would find no hindrance from the Duarte Government. They would be welcome. The workers then would have to choose between starvation or starvation wages along with toxic substances. So it is immoral, as the Hon. Member has suggested, and I hope it will be looked at seriously in committee.

Madam Speaker, 1 would like to thank the Hon. Member for his answer, which was as thoughtful as usual. On the domestic front, and I refer particularly to Manitoba, two of its major rivers, the Assiniboine River and the Red River, are seriously contaminated with toxic chemical substances. The Government of that province is reluctant to take the necessary action. It being a New Democratic Government, that may not be good news to the Hon. Member for Spadina. Nevertheless, I would have to put to him the following question: Since the Government of that province is not doing what the Hon. Member, I am sure, would like that Government, and also the Government of Canada, to do, namely, to clean up and to prevent the pollution of toxic chemicals of major waterways in that province, does the Hon. Member see in this particular Bill the means to intervene in the Province of Manitoba to get the New Democratic Government there to do the things which are needed in order to clean up the pollution of toxic chemicals in those two major rivers?

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member was speaking about a city that I know because I was born there and I grew up there. I was very familiar with those two rivers, the Red and the Assiniboine. When I swam in them when 1 am was a kid they were dirty enough, but I would not swim in them now. I believe this Bill, and this was the main point I was making at the beginning of my remarks, does not provide for clear responsibility by the federal Government. I am not familiar with the current discussions in Manitoba about the action for remedying the quality of the water caused by pollution in those two rivers.
The situation at present is that there is no federal responsibility, as 1 said when I was describing what happened in Toronto a decade ago. After this Bill has been passed there may or may not be effective federal responsibility. I am not clear on that. My colleagues are not clear on that either. We are not clear as to whether or not it will simply provide for buck passing. I think that in both cases, whether it is between a provincial Government such as a Liberal one, a New Democratic one or a Tory one, and the federal Government, there will be attempts to pass the administrative costs of the remedial action to the other level of Government. That is why I wish that this Bill would more clearly assert the obligation of
October 23, 1987

the federal Government to act if the provincial Government does not.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: If there are no more questions or comments, we will resume debate with the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young).

Madam Speaker, I want to spend a few minutes on this particular matter given its importance, not only to the people of Canada but on a global scale.
First, I think it is unfortunate that the Government really missed an opportunity here by coming forward with the kind of Bill that it has come forward with. There was absolutely no public discussion prior to the Government, or the Minister in this case, drafting this particular piece of legislation. I think that is also very unfortunate.
The Government, like most others, for some reason when it comes to environmental concerns seems to feel that it and only it has the knowledge and the authority to deal with environmental problems. In fact, usually the response to environmental concerns is that the person raising those concerns is just trying to frighten the general public, or that the concern that has been identified is really not as critical as people say it is.
I want to give two or three examples of this which might be helpful. A number of years ago I had the opportunity to chair a task force that went down to the Niagara Peninsula to take a look at what was happening to the Niagara River as a result of chemical dump sites. These were located primarily on the New York side of the Niagara River and were, first, located in the worst place that they could possibly be located and, second, they were too close to that river. As a result of these locations, and particularly because the excavations rested on dolomite rock which, as you probably know, Madam Speaker, is a highly porous rock, these toxic wastes had begun to seep through the rock into the underground water system and were leaching into the Niagara River.
I want to tell the House that the people in those communities had become quite fearful for their own safety over the years and had gone to some great lengths to try to convince Governments, both at the provincial and the federal level, that this was a matter that deserved some attention. By the way, these were people whom I would class as probably being in very upper middle class income groups who were expressing those concerns. They were people who had never protested anything in their lives and who felt that if they spoke in a reasonable way to Governments, they would respond to their approach. They found something quite different.
They found that Governments did not respond for a whole variety of reasons which I do not want to take the time to go into now. But the Governments in fact did not respond to these concerns. Some of those groups were forced to take some actions which, for them, were quite revolutionary to raise public awareness and to bring some media attention to the
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
views that they were expressing. They had real reason for concern.
Across the river from many of these communities was the Hyde Park dump site, which was also a part of the same corporation, the Hooker Chemical Corporation, which had been largely responsible for the Love Canal travesty. I want to tell you, Madam Speaker, when I went over to take a look at that Love Canal site I had imagined a small community, a small village or something like that. This was a whole subdivision of houses that had been built and constructed on this chemical dump site and which had been discovered largely through the work of Dr. Beverly Paigen, who had acquaintances who actually lived in the community on the Love Canal site. She had heard about the high incidence of cancer in that community, as well as the highly abnormal defects in births in that community, and she did some work on that. In fact, she was the person who brought it to the attention of the public.
That whole Love Canal community is now ringed off by wire fencing. People cannot get access to it, naturally, because the basements are now flooded with chemical wastes. I want to tell the House that after I took a look at that community and saw what could happen to other communities around the Niagara River site, and other members of that committee were with me and saw it, I left there in complete shock. It raised my interest in environmental concerns a great deal.
I want to talk about one simple thing that means a great deal to my own community in the east end of Toronto. Not so very long ago kids could go down into Lake Ontario during the summer months to swim. One cannot do that any more. One cannot do that any more because of the pollution in Lake Ontario along the bottom of my own constituency in Beaches and along Broadview-Greenwood. One cannot swim on most of the recreational beaches in Metropolitan Toronto in the summer months any more because of the pollution in that lake.
There would be a very simple solution to that problem, if Governments had the political will to do something about it. Most of the pollution that I am referring to comes largely as a result of overflows in the storm sewage system. For years it has been recognized that the whole sewage system should be separated in order that the regular waste sewage does not overflow during heavy thunderstorms, for example, in the summer months.
The Federation of Canadian Municipalities made a recommendation to the federal Government within the last year that called for an expenditure-and it is not only in Metropolitan Toronto, but also in other large metropolitan communities-of some $12 billion over a five-year period that could be shared by municipal, provincial, and federal Governments. It is my understanding that the provinces and municipalities have agreed to enter into such a cost-sharing agreement. However, the federal Government refuses to do so, on the basis that if municipalities see a need to upgrade those

October 23, 1987
Organized Crime
sewer systems, then they should raise taxes at the municipal level, or do something else to raise the taxes in order that they could do the work themselves.
The federal Government ignores the environmental concerns. It also chooses to ignore the fact that part of this proposal clearly showed that, if the federal Government entered into such an agreement, some 60,000 jobs a year could be created over a five-year period as a result of that effort to clean up the environment. Governments are extremely shortsighted when looking at environmental concerns, and when looking at proposals that will not only clean up the environment but will create jobs in the process.
On the task force that I was on, I had the opportunity to take a look at a chemical producing plant in Sarnia, Ontario, where there was extremely bad pollution, especially air pollution coming out of that plant, a number of years ago. The employer was persuaded by environmental groups and the Ontario Government of the day to clean up that plant. When 1 was there, there was a whole display inside the plant about pollution control equipment. The company now boasts that, as a result of cleaning up the environment on that work site, it created new additional jobs and new technologies for that particular corporation. Cleaning up the environment can also be a job creation project. It is not only a question of expending money, jobs can also be created in the process of doing a socially useful thing.
In conclusion, I wish to state that the environment does not belong to us to abuse, destroy, and to use as some kind of large sewage waste disposal system. Our environment is only borrowed by us for future generations. As elected representatives and people who can do something about environmental concerns, we have a responsibility to act on them in that type of principle.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the last time I referred briefly to the situation of organized crime in our country.

In the seven minutes available today I wish to deal with the question of the current crime trend, the extent of hard drug trafficking in this country, and something about the Kefauver Commission in the United States which dealt with the matter proposed in the motion, namely, that there be a royal commission to look at organized crime in this country.
October 23, 1987

The crime rate nationally is up. For violent crime it is up approximately 31 per cent across Canada. In Manitoba, violent crime appears to be up about 84 per cent in that province since 1980. From the latest statistics, it is up approximately 45 per cent in Saskatchewan, 33 per cent in Ontario, and property crimes are up in seven of the ten provinces. In Vancouver, the crime rate is up to approximately 35 per cent. Why is this? Is this because of organized crime, or is this because of spontaneous crime perhaps due to unemployment or some other cause? What part of the present crime has been created by organized crime, which I define as being crime organized by two or more people, and not something spontaneous?
That brings us to the illegal drug problem in our country which has been worsening now for several years. The RCMP estimate that the amount of illegal drugs sold in this country is now in the $10 billion a year range, which is more than the sales of General Motors each year. I know that some people dispute that figure. Worldwide illegal drug sales have been estimated to be in the trillion dollar range. One of the questions that comes out of that is, who will control our domestic industries 20 years from now, if illegal drug people continue to pocket that type of money, tax free, year after year, and to invest it as they like in whatever they like?
1 am told by the RCMP that a substantial portion of a large new development in one of our major cities is now being financed by recycled drug proceeds. Not very long ago an individual in the Province of British Columbia was found to have $3.2 million in probable drug money in a suitcase. A heroin drug ring in the City of Montreal has removed an estimated tens of millions of dollars from this country during a two-year period. Hon. Members will recall that 30 tons or tonnes-I do not know if it was metric or not-of hashish were seized not long ago off our East Coast. In short, unless we try some new approaches, the problems of hard drugs are likely to worsen as time goes by.
One excellent manner to start, and I am speaking as a former Crown Attorney, is Bill C-61 which has been introduced in the House and received second reading. It provides an effective anti-drug push, and it is something that Canadians would like us to pass.
As the law presently stands, if an individual has $1 million in his bank account obtained from illegal drug profits, unless that money can be shown to have been part of his method of doing the crime or directly linked to the crime no one can touch that money. The proposed law would give us the chance to seize such property, real estate, bank accounts, and the like, which is the only way ultimately to get at drug traffickers. In other words, the philosophy should be like the English common law. If I buy a million dollar insurance policy on my wife, then I murder my wife, I should not be entitled to have the million dollar proceeds.
The search provisions in the Bill are important; the ability to seize money and property. Under the Bill, if passed, what is
Organized Crime
called the in rem clause is important because if an accused person dies or leaves the country, under the Bill if passed, his assets may be seized. What motivates drug traffickers is known to be one thing, money. A young person said not long ago, "I can make a million dollars selling drugs and the state will never touch it", an RCMP drug enforcement person reported. Forfeiting drug profits must be the major focus of beefing up our legislation. An effective in rem clause similar to the one in the U.S. legislation would help us do that. It would also be consistent with our Charter of Rights, just as the American provision has been found to be consistent with its Bill of Rights.
It seems to me to make sense to confine the new forfeiture provision to drug matters only because all of us take a serious view of drug trafficking. If we expanded into too many other things the banks and others would get excited about it. It might be wise to restrict the provision just to drug trafficking.
A matter which might be looked at by a royal commission is the question of heroin arriving by mail. Canada is one of the few countries that does not allow people, up to a year or so ago, to open the mail no matter how overwhelming the indication is that a particular letter or package contains heroin. We should obtain a provision whereby, with a judge's order and overwhelming evidence that an envelope contains heroin, the Government should be allowed to open such mail it seems to me.
I recall speaking to a customs officer a few years ago who suggested that thousands of letters come into Canada every year containing heroin. If the motion is passed I hope the commission would look into that because it is a very serious problem, particularly for our young people. Again, if I may try to drive the point home, a study in the United States found that 237 heroin addicts in the City of Baltimore over a 10 or 11 year period committed half a million crimes in that city.
I have defended these addicts. They simply have to rob seven days a week in many cases if they are heroin addicts in order to have the money to pay $50 or $100 for two caps of heroin a day.
May I draw the House's attention to the Kefauver U.S. Senate committee report of 1951. That commission dealt with the extent to which:
Gangsters and racketeers continue to pursue their vicious careers and invest
the spoils of their illegitimate activity in legitimate enterprises.
I know that was 30 years ago in another country, but the principle, it seems to me, is, unfortunately, still valid today in Canada. The Kefauver committee found that the professional criminals in the United States were putting that money into the liquor industry, banking and finance. Two of the commission's recommendations were, one, that personnel of federal law enforcement agencies should be materially increased, their salaries increased. I think our own law enforcement people would like to see that done too. Two, a racket squad should be

October 23, 1987
Organized Crime
organized in the U.S. Justice Department. Perhaps if this commission were appointed it might wish to recommend that too.
In short, I think there is much to recommend the suggestion by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson).

speechtext:
Organized crime is prevalent in our country although it is hard to tell how deep and in what particular regions it is more so than in others.
In the areas of importation, manufacturing and distribution of narcotics, and illicit drugs in the drug trade, the Hon. Member for Edmonton talked about the tragedy of the need for heroin. It is a terrible problem. The Member has prosecuted and maybe defended, as I have, people who have been charged with heroin possession and with trafficking. They are basically sick people but they are also robbers, but one has to think of the victims, something we have never fully dealt with in Canada. We have never really dealt with the problem of legalization and whether we could use the British model. However, it has all sorts of problems. There is no easy answer. The Member was right in identifying it as being part of the problem. What about the people who manipulate the addicts and earn tremendous profit? That problem has to be attacked continually.
Then we have hijacking and prostitution. In the area of pornography we think the Government's new Bill on pornography will force more of this type of thing underground, not so much the really bad stuff, because that is there anyway, but erotica which could be classed illegal. There are some dangers to that. It could go underground and organized crime would become involved. Escort services, gambling and even in the video poker game machines organized crime has been known to get involved. Then we have the smuggling of aliens and immigrants, the terrorizing and extortion of immigrants, and
the extortion of small business. What about car thefts, armed robberies, fencing of goods, arson and stolen securities? The whole area of white-collar crime is there.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) speaking in the House on May 4, 1987, made reference to a prison. He said that if a prison had only white-collar criminals in it, how different it would be because people in prison tend to be lower-income and poor people. The Member from Burnaby talked quite eloquently in reference to this Bill the one time it was debated. He said that we need to look into the whole matter of white-collar crime, environmental crime, and pollution in terms of criminal offences. We need to look into the whole area of worker safety and the kind of safety provided for workers. What about people who do not pay minimum wages and try to get away with it? We have not thought of those things as crime although they are. We would like to see that aspect broadened.
I am from Vancouver and I do not know whether Members are aware but there is another area that should be looked into, namely that of gangs. We have heard and saw a lot on television about motorcycle gangs and the wars between the gangs in the Province of Quebec. We saw pictures of bodies that were pulled out of the St. Lawrence River. I had a young boy in my riding, 16 years of age, who had been in and out of school. His mother came home a month or so ago and found him bound, gagged and shot to death in her apartment. The police believe the slaying had to do with one of the gangs in Vancouver. This is pretty tragic stuff and it goes far beyond the normal activities of juvenile gangs, the kind of activities we have seen in the past.
Vancouver is about where San Francisco was 10 years ago, with inter-gang rivalries possibly leading to violence. The Coordinated Law Enforcement Unit in British Columbia, a branch of the police force, identify a number of gangs and say that there are about 200 people involved in the city's major gangs, which include the Lotus-Jung Ching Gang, the Red Eagles, the Viet Ching and the Big Circle. The Attorney General of British Columbia has just appointed a 14-member unit, which costs about $800,000 a year, to look into these gangs and try to bring these people to justice.
Two and a half years ago, Jim and Lily Ming, restaurant owners, were kidnapped and brutally slain in a ransom bid case in Vancouver. I do not believe that that case has been solved.
In my area of the country, there is a growing problem with gangs, and not just juvenile gangs. There has always been a problem, as the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) said, with narcotics. He and I used to work in a building which was located on a street called The Corner at Main and Pender. Especially at Main and Hastings, the whole narcotics and heroin trade was centred around that area about 15 years ago. Unfortunately, that trade has expanded so that we cannot identify just one corner. Organized crime is
October 23, 1987

manipulating the drug trade, the protection rackets and the thefts. Those things have to be looked into.
I will not say much more about that. I congratulate the Hon. Member for Trinity on her motion. 1 would like to see its terms of reference expanded so that it would look into gangs and also consider the nature of white-collar crime. I was going to say that white-collar crime is growing, but 1 do not think it is growing, it is just not prosecuted enough. We tend to prosecute the poor people rather than the rich. There is sometimes one law for the rich and a different law for the poor. The breaking of pollution and environmental laws and some of the securities frauds affect all of us. We are all victims of those crimes, and that area should be looked into as well.
Again, I congratulate the Hon. Member on her motion. Let us not be satisfied with the Bills the Government has brought in which, as government Members have pretended, will solve some of the problems, because they will not.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very happy to have an opportunity to speak to the motion of the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), a highly respected member of this place. She has presented an important motion to us today. As Chairman of the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General, I want to congratulate her particularly for drawing to the attention of the House and of the people of Canada this very important matter.
Our Government is certainly well aware of the problem of organized crime and my colleagues on this side of the House will be discussing this afternoon some of the many initiatives this Government has taken in combatting organized crime. There has been improved legislation, enhanced resources, improved systems of collecting, analysing and disseminating intelligence on organized crime and as well as new arrangements with foreign Governments.
I want to focus my remarks on one part of the Hon. Member's motion, part 6, which calls upon the House to consider the advisability of appointing a royal commission to investigate organized crime in Canada and to include in its report observations and recommendations on a number of matters, including possible guidelines for enforcement agencies in dealing with witnesses against organized crime. 1 think the Hon. Member has quite rightly focused on an important part of the question.
1 would point out to my colleagues that this is a matter which is currently being examined by the Ministry of the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kelleher). It is being examined by his Department in collaboration with provincial Attorneys General and Solicitors General and other federal Ministers concerned with law enforcement issues.
I think we all agree that witness protection is part and parcel of a serious commitment on the part of the Government and law enforcement agencies to pursue forcefully organized criminal activities. I am sure some Hon. Members are aware
Organized Crime
that in the United States, the federal Government instituted a witness protection program aimed at organized crime. This program is administered by the United States marshals' service.
The need for a wide-ranging formal program in the United States is, I would suggest, based on the magnitude of the organized crime problem there. Fortunately, we in Canada are not faced with a problem of a similar magnitude. That is not to suggest, however, that it is not a significant problem worth addressing.
Hon. Members are of course aware that the administration of justice is a provincial responsibility and as a consequence, the majority of witnesses requiring protection or relocation, perhaps even new identities, are the responsibility and, will continue to be so of provincial authorities. The federal Government, through the RCMP and other federal Departments, does, however, provide assistance to provincial officials in the form of documentation required for the witnesses to establish new identities. The RCMP also assists other police forces in other aspects of witness protection.
These flexible arrangements which provide for witness protection have been generally satisfactory, I would suggest, in meeting the needs of Canadians over the last number of years. Hon. Members will appreciate that the Government and departmental officials are constantly monitoring the effectiveness of the various programs, however, and of the arrangements related to law enforcement in general and organized crime in particular.
Witness protection has been identified as an area requiring examination. As 1 mentioned earlier, this examination is in progress by the Ministry of the Solicitor General and provincial representatives.
In considering this matter, the Government is proceeding carefully, and so it should. The arrangements pertaining to witness protection must ultimately serve to increase the number of successful prosecutions of those criminal cases where there are threats of intimidation or violence against witnesses and their families which are occasioned by the implicated criminal group.
The arrangements must also serve to increase the willingness of witnesses to reveal and testify about criminal offences of which they have some knowledge. In this context, it is important to determine the principles of the arrangements, the eligibility criteria for witnesses and the range of services that should be afforded witnesses who testify against organized crime groups.
Earlier I referred to the witness protection program in the United States. It is generally acknowledged by American officials and academics that their program experienced considerable difficulty and growing pains. Let me just mention some of the problems.

October 23, 1987
Organized Crime
First, there is under-funding and under-resourcing. Then there is difficulty in relocating and changing the identity of professionals. If you are a doctor or businessman it is pretty hard to change your profession. Adverse publicity for the program has been experienced. Then there is the problem of the commission of criminal offences by witnesses after relocation and change of identity, a very serious problem, I understand. They also have to ensure that the new identity is not used as a shield to evade creditors. There are problems resulting from separation and divorce of program participants, and access to children. There is failure to develop the required expertise, that is counselling and administrative services, rapidly enough to prepare the witness properly to adjust to the new life and new job. There are difficulties in providing identification documentation. Generally speaking, there is a careless, insensitive and unsympathetic attitude to the witness' trauma and problems in re-establishing themselves.
Given the U.S. experience we can appreciate that the administration of witness protection is difficult, often distasteful, and always unrewarding as the vast majority of witnesses in such programs are themselves criminals. The RCMP experience has included many of those difficulties. It is important that Governments and enforcement authorities bear these experiences in mind when considering any new arrangements to protect organized crime witnesses.
In closing, the important point is that the issue of witness protection is under careful consideration by both federal and provincial authorities. The motion, in referring to the advisability of appointing a royal commission to inquire into this matter, seems to be somewhat superfluous. I believe such an inquiry would not add substantially to our existing knowledge, something which is being added to in our current consultations and inquiries. It would in fact run the risk of unnecessarily consuming scarce resources and perhaps even delaying achievement of the objective which I am sure Members on all sides want to achieve. I simply urge caution on the part of the Hon. Member for Trinity and other Members in considering whether or not they should support this motion, at least parts of the motion.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if I may, I will preface my remarks by adding my commendation to that of my friend of the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) for her concern over a matter which really concerns all of us, the impact of organized crime on Canadian society. It is rather trite to say that this phenomenon is a plague on practically all democratic Governments. We all read the papers and know that fortunes have reportedly been amassed by those unscrupulous and evil persons at the expense of the weak or desperate in our society.
I have been most impressed by the quality of the speeches made so far in this debate. They show the concern Members have about the continuance of organized crime in this country we call Canada. I sense a genuine will to put some truth into
the old adage that crime does not pay. Unfortunately, all too often it has been seen that crime does sometimes pay.
Honest businessmen, friends of yours and mine, are lured by greed and the prospect of immense profits to join hands with disreputable representatives of the underworld. In addition to the obvious motive of greed, experience has shown that a sense of adventure and intrigue has seduced some of these dupes who are not even aware that they themselves are becoming snagged in the murderous tentacles of formidable criminal organizations until it is too late.
In Canada, with our constant exposure to graphic depictions of the presence of organized criminal activities in the American news media, as well as the well-publicized domestic examples, we have come to view the presence of such rogues much as bathers who recognize that predator sharks often lurk out of sight beneath the surface of the ocean only metres from the shore; cold, unfeeling and ready to take advantage when the opportunity presents itself. Just as counter-measures have been found to protect those who flock to the beaches every summer, I am confident that effective counter-measures will be developed to address this scourge of criminal organizations intent on operating against the interests of Canadian society.
Many Canadians will remember that Members of this House have on several occasions sought to improve the Criminal Code so as to improve the effectiveness of those practical tools, such as electronic surveillance, which are employed by the police. There has been continuing cooperation and consultation between the provincial authorities and federal officials in this area.
As several Members who participated in this debate pointed out, the Government is very much aware of the problem of organized crime in Canada and internationally. They discussed examples of Canada's participation with other states in agreements intended to stymie international criminal conspiracies. Mention was made of the sufficiency of present legislation in regard to the punishment of criminal conspiracy to murder. I respectfully agree with the views advanced by the Hon. Member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Duplessis). By providing that the maximum penalty that may be imposed for such offences is life imprisonment, the Parliament of Canada has signaled how serious it considers such acts, and created an appropriate sanction for such an offence.
Mention was made of the thorough federal-provincial analysis of the role of organized crime completed in June of 1983, as well as proposals that legislation be created to take effective action to trace, seize and confiscate the fruits of crime. That is one more step in the enforcement of the law in order to ensure that crime does not pay.
It is clear that the Government has recognized the threat to Canadian society in general, and the criminal justice system in particular, posed by the perception that fortunes are being made through the exploitation of the drug trade, loan sharking, extortion and other nefarious activities by persons and
October 23, 1987

groups who have remained, thus far, insulated from the heat of police investigation or other criminal prosecution.
I share the view of a previous speaker who ventured the opinion that there really is no need to ask a royal commission to examine this matter, both because of the substantial costs involved, as well as the fact that scant information not already in possession of law enforcement officials would likely be developed.
I have no doubt that such an inquiry would prove fascinating for the general law-abiding citizen and extremely lucrative to the media-which would be expected to keep us informed on the daily developments-and perhaps the legal profession. However, just as the disclosure of any piece of information may endanger the life of a spy in intelligence matters, the public disclosure of many pieces of information relating to criminal organizations might put the lives of informers at significant risk.
In closing, I would like to echo the belief previously expressed in this debate that the precious resources existing in this country to combat crime would be better utilized in the investigation and prosecution of criminal conspiracies rather than in the protracted hearings of a royal commission which would, as has been said so frequently before, not likely provide knowledge which federal and provincial criminal intelligence resources had not already provided to authorities.
1 do not minimize the issue, Madam Speaker. As I indicated at the outset, I commend the Hon. Member for Trinity for bringing this matter forward, but I sincerely believe that it is in the interest of all Canadians that proposed legislation to address the proceeds of crime and deal effectively with drug traffickers not be retarded or delayed in any way.
The Government initiatives, mentioned on earlier occasions, will, I am sure, be welcomed by all Members in this House who believe that concerted efforts are required now to reduce the mayhem caused by organized crime in this great country of ours. Now is the time to start an action program.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I intend to speak for a few moments about organized crime and that part of Motion M-44 which proposes that this House appoint a royal commission that would conduct an investigation and make recommendations on legislation to enable the Government to identify and appropriate the proceeds of organized crime.
First of all, I think the Hon. Member is to be commended for the interest she has shown in this matter. All Members present undoubtedly understand how important it is to society that our laws allow for confiscation of the proceeds of crime.
Organized crime may take the form of a more or less permanent understanding between individuals, for their mutual benefit, as in the case of crime syndicates which have
Organized Crime
specific criteria for their membership and an established organizational structure. This definition can also apply to individuals who join forces for a single transaction or even to individuals acting independently.
There have always been people who, either alone or with others, have chosen the path of crime to reach their goals. In most cases, our penal laws have, in the past, provided adequate redress through the use of traditional sanctions such as fines and imprisonment.
However, during the second half of the twentieth century there has been a marked increase in profit-related crime, of which drug trafficking is an excellent example. There is no comparison between this new kind of crime and the kind with which our predecessors had to contend when they drafted our penal laws. There are even individuals, some with no previous record, who are willing to risk arrest and conviction, even when the law provides a maximum penalty of life imprisonment.
Madam Speaker, these people are prepared to risk a jail term because of the enormous profits generated by drug trafficking. The illegal profits involved in certain crimes are so great that there are certain national and international crime organizations that devote all their energies to the perpetration of these crimes. These organizations take advantage of today's modern communications, means of transportation and banking procedures, and the limited jurisdiction of national legal systems to amass illicit wealth.
The Criminal Code contains several provisions allowing for the confiscation of various items, the possession of which is illegal. These include restricted firearms, obscene publications, hate propaganda and counterfeit money.
The provisions, however, apply only to the tools used to perpetrate an offence and to possession of smuggled items. They do not provide for confiscating the illicit proceeds of-

Madam Speaker, it is rather interesting that in debate on this issue we are all saying that it is a very laudable motion and that we are very excited that the Member has brought it forward, yet each one of us in turn is giving reasons why we should not do this. We know that there is a problem in Canada. We know that there are socially unacceptable elements operating in our communities. We know that organized crime has a foothold in our society. We are groping to find the best way to fight that.

October 23, 1987
Organized Crime
The biggest problem is that a royal commission would cost a great deal of money. I, for one, believe that that money should be spent trying to solve the problem by working with the people in our communities so that they are not vulnerable to those involved in organized crime.
The Government of Canada is making a great effort to fight organized crime through various Departments.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) will soon be tabling legislation in the House to implement mutual legal assistance treaties with other countries, which will include provisions designed to promote joint investigations aimed at curtailing organized criminal activity. This initiative was announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in the Throne Speech. The pending legislation will enable the Government to identify and appropriate the proceeds of crime, thereby taking the profit out of some of the activities involved therein.
Currently the RCMP participates with provincial and municipal police forces in investigations of organized crime. There have been many situations in New Brunswick recently in which investigations involving the RCMP and provincial and municipal police have resulted in the apprehension of a great number of people involved in drug trafficking. We are seeing more and more instances of co-operation between Governments as they jointly try to cope with the spread of organized crime, particularly in the area of drug trafficking.
The RCMP co-ordinated the publication of an annual report, the Criminal Intelligence Service of Canada, which reports on organized criminal activities in all jurisdictions throughout Canada. They are providing the information to municipal and provincial police forces so that they, in turn, can get the benefit of the work being done by the RCMP in collecting statistics in this area.
It is recognized by the Government that drugs have become the focus of many organized crime activities in this country. As a result, the RCMP drug enforcement program employed a force of 999 persons located in 122 federal units from coast to coast during 1985 and 1986. Detachments which have no dedicated drug units also have a responsibility to enforce laws pertaining to illicit drugs and the trafficking thereof.
Furthermore, the Speech from the Throne referred to the government initiative in the area of developing and implementing a national drug strategy. The secretariat of the Solicitor General has worked with officials of the RCMP, the Departments of Justice and National Health and Welfare to develop mechanisms to improve federal and international efforts to combat drug trafficking and use.
Obviously much can be done with the money that would be spent on a royal commission. As a municipal politician, I can think of the advantages to the citizens of my particular city when our police officers were able to come to Ottawa for the
training programs that were being put forward by the Solicitor General and the RCMP to train them in surveillance, the apprehension of those trafficking in drugs, and to train them in the proper methods by which they will charge someone with the offence. These programs were extremely beneficial to those communities and would be an excellent use of additional funds from the Government of Canada.
We can also think of those who are perhaps most vulnerable to the activities of organized crime. They include the less fortunate and young people, such as those who rely on teenage prostitution for support. There are young people in our society who do not steal for pleasure but because they need food.
I was an educator in New Brunswick in 1970. One of my 13-year old students was stealing lunches from other students and stealing from neighbourhood houses. He was not taking anything that he would use for pleasure, or stealing money that he would use for selfish purposes; he was looking for food. Since there obviously was not enough support at home to meet the needs of that child, he made himself vulnerable to others who might encourage him to get into criminal activities.
We must make an effort to put the money where it will work in our communities, through our social agencies and local police forces in order to fight poverty, social injustice, and remove some of the causes that make young people particularly, but also anyone else in our society, vulnerable to the activities of organized crime.
While a royal commission may be a nice idea and an attractive mechanism by which the Government can say it is doing something, I think we all realize it would not accomplish much. If the money for such a royal commission is available, it should be provided to the provinces and municipalities to give greater professional training to those involved in fighting crime and give greater opportunities to those who may be less fortunate and therefore more vulnerable to the activities of organized crime and the lure that it presents.
I believe that Canadians want results, rather than the showcase of another royal commission. In order to achieve those results we must go to the root of the problems which exist in every community of this country. We have an obligation as Members of Parliament to direct federal money in the area where it will give the most advantages and best long-term results in fighting organized crime.

Madam Speaker, before speaking to the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), I should like to commend her for drawing the attention of the House to the question of organized crime.

While there may be some merit in the Hon. Member's suggestion for a royal commission, there are other matters which should be considered. For example, it is time for the introduction of effective legislative apparatus to confiscate the
October 23, 1987

proceeds of crime. This Government fully supports such an endeavour because the time for action has arrived. Any further delay will distance Canada from the efforts of virtually all other western democracies to limit the growth of these criminal umpires. Because of the absence of such legislation in Canada, we would appear to the criminal element to be a haven for such activity when compared with our international partners.

Madam Speaker, 1 would be remiss if I failed to mention the efforts made by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and other provincial and municipal police forces.
Indeed, each year at the Canadian Police College the RCMP provide training for policemen from the four corners of the world and send experts to various countries, including Commonwealth nations, where they teach the skills required to fight against the different types of crime now under consideration in the House. Canadian law enforcement officials, particularly RCMP officers, work in close co-operation with their counterparts in other western democratic countries to fight against every kind of crime, especially organized crime which knows no borders.
We can readily appreciate the legitimate concerns of the Hon. Member over organized crime. However, Canada is still at one with the provinces when it comes to renewed law enforcement efforts, and a royal commission would contribute precious little to existing or soon to be implemented fight mechanisms.
Organized Crime
Madam Speaker, I realize that the motion sponsored by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) attests to deep concern about the extent of organized crime in Canada and the weakness of law enforcement measures, but I want to assure her that the members of Canada's police community and other devoted criminal justice experts are dealing with the problem with utmost competence. Our Government has confidence in them, and they deserve the support of all Hon. Members and of the Canadian public at large.
